exam: A 12‑year‑old boy from a rural Kenyan village presents with pallor, eosinophilia, and Hb 8 g/dL. What is your next step? — Empiric albendazole and iron, because microscopy may be unavailable and disease severity warrants treatment.

How does the life cycle of Ancylostoma duodenale explain the classic ‘ground itch’ symptom? — Larvae penetrate skin, causing a localized pruritic papule; recognizing this helps link exposure to disease.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester has mild anemia and works barefoot. Which anti‑helminthic is safest? — Albendazole is acceptable after the first trimester; praziquantel is not indicated for hookworm.
What laboratory finding can be misleading in early hookworm infection? — Normal hemoglobin early on; anemia may develop weeks after infection, so clinical suspicion remains key.
Why is iron supplementation essential even after successful deworming? — Hookworms cause chronic blood loss; iron stores need replenishment to resolve anemia fully.

Differentiate hookworm anemia from anemia of chronic disease in a patient with HIV. — Hookworm shows iron‑deficiency pattern (low ferritin, high TIBC), while chronic disease shows normal/high ferritin and low TIBC.
What public‑health measure most reduces transmission in low‑resource settings? — Promoting shoe wearing and safe fecal disposal; mass deworming campaigns are secondary.

A patient with severe anemia is found to have both hookworm and schistosomiasis. How does this affect management? — Treat both parasites (albendazole + praziquantel) and prioritize rapid correction of anemia.
ai.title: Ancylostoma duodenale Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Hookworm infection by Ancylostoma duodenale causes chronic intestinal blood loss and anemia, especially in low‑resource settings. Understanding transmission, diagnosis without advanced labs, and pragmatic treatment is essential for ward‑rounds.

b: Most common in children and agricultural workers
sections.p: Ancylostoma duodenale is a soil‑transmitted nematode endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, notably East Africa. Infection is acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil and leads to chronic iron‑deficiency anemia.

b: Eggs are oval, thick‑shelled, and embryonated in stool
Larvae are rhabditiform in stool, filariform in soil
sections.p: A slender, reddish‑brown roundworm about 10‑13 mm long in the adult female. It has buccal teeth that allow it to attach to the intestinal mucosa and feed on blood.

b: Skin contact with contaminated sand or barefoot walking
Poor sanitation and use of human feces as fertilizer
sections.p: Infective filariform larvae penetrate intact skin, travel via the bloodstream to the lungs, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature in the duodenum.

Chronic intestinal blood loss produces iron‑deficiency anemia, eosinophilia, and sometimes protein‑losing enteropathy. Heavy infection can cause severe anemia, growth failure, and, rarely, intestinal obstruction.

b: If microscopy unavailable, treat empirically when anemia + eosinophilia in endemic area
sections.p: Microscopy of a single stool sample may miss low‑intensity infection; concentration techniques improve yield. In low‑resource settings, clinical suspicion plus anemia and eosinophilia guide treatment.

t.b: Detects eggs → confirms infection; negative does not exclude low‑burden disease
Shows chronic blood loss; supports hookworm as cause of anemia
Eosinophilia > 500/µL suggests helminth infection; low Hb quantifies severity

sections.p: Single‑dose albendazole or mebendazole is recommended; they are inexpensive, oral, and safe in pregnancy after the first trimester. Iron supplementation and nutrition improve recovery.

t.b: Assesses response; rising Hb over weeks indicates successful therapy
Confirms cure; not required if clinical improvement evident

b: Key clue: barefoot farmer with iron‑deficiency anemia and eosinophilia
Differential includes: Trichuris trichiura (less blood loss), Schistosoma mansoni (portal hypertension signs)
sections.p: Focus on epidemiology, the skin‑penetration route, anemia pattern, and pragmatic management without sophisticated labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL) with tachycardia or hypotension
Signs of heart failure from chronic anemia
